paras: The lynching of Henry Caldwell took place shortly after midnight on July 30, 1882, when a disguised mob took Caldwell, a Black man held on a charge of assaulting an elderly white woman, from the Iron County jail at Ironton, Missouri, and hanged and shot him from the Iron Mountain Railroad bridge. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of a mob whose members were unknown to it. The local weekly endorsed the killing, while St. Louis wire reports carried it to papers across the country under headlines such as 'A Ravisher Lynched.'

Caldwell lived on Zion's Hill in Ironton, and in May 1882 the Iron County Register described him as 'at times out-and-out crazy' after Marshal Patton arrested him for threatening his family; he was fined for carrying concealed weapons.

On the morning of Thursday, July 27, Caldwell was accused of attacking Mrs. Peck, a white woman over sixty, in the yard of her house. According to the Register, Mr. Delano of the Blue Store raised the alarm, and C. W. Tetwiler, John Phoebe, described as 'colored,' and others ran to the house and took Caldwell after a struggle. Judge Dinger held a preliminary examination the next day and bound him over to the Circuit Court in the sum of $10,000. Threats of lynching were 'freely made' at the arrest, according to the wire report.

Sheriff Bill Fletcher had kept watch on the two previous nights but not on Saturday, when around midnight, the Register reported, thirty or forty men with masks or blackened faces gathered on Main Street, were 'sworn in' to silence, and marched to the jail; wire reports put the party at about a hundred. The men broke the lock of the inner iron door with an ax, held the sheriff at gunpoint, took the cell key from him, and led Caldwell out with a noose around his neck.

At the railroad bridge southeast of Ironton the mob tied the rope to a beam and threw Caldwell over the parapet. When he clung to the timbers, a knife slash through his arm broke his hold, and because his feet touched the ground the men fired some thirty shots into him before dispersing. One wire version said Caldwell 'begged piteously for his life' and was shoved off the hand rail, and it did not mention the shooting.

Coroner Grandhomme summoned a jury at one o'clock that morning and cut the body down; with Constable Patton he brought it to the Court House, and after lying in the sheriff's room until ten o'clock it was buried in the potter's field. The jury, with Jos. F. Lindsay as foreman, found that Caldwell had been taken by force from lawful custody and killed by a mob whose members were 'unknown to us.'

A week later the Register reported that a squad of men had gathered in Ironton's streets to 'punish' another resident, and in an editorial headed 'MOB LAW' it warned that further mob action would not be tolerated, even as it called Caldwell's lynching 'not without excuse.'

The fullest account came from the Iron County Register, which headed its story 'A Terrible Crime and its Reward,' called Caldwell a 'black brute,' and wrote that if any case called 'justly' for lynch law, 'this was one.' On August 10 the paper reprinted a Cincinnati Times-Star jibe that some Ironton citizens went to church that Sunday while others 'lynched a negro.'

Outside Missouri, the story ran on July 31 as a St. Louis dispatch in the Omaha Daily Bee, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and other dailies, under headlines such as 'A Ravisher Lynched' and 'Negro Lynched for Attempted Rape' that stated the accusation as fact. The Sacramento version placed the event at 'Canton, Mo.,' an apparent wire error. Weekly news summaries from Pennsylvania to Mississippi later reduced the case to one line naming Caldwell, Ironton and the masked men.

The size of the mob differs by source: the Register counted thirty or forty men, while the St. Louis wire said about a hundred; the local paper, which names the meeting place and describes the oath, is the closer account.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Caldwell
bases: A disguised mob took Caldwell, held on a charge of assaulting a white woman, from the Iron County jail and hanged and shot him from a railroad bridge (A10, A11, A12).

A mob of thirty to forty (local paper) or about a hundred (wire) men forced the jail, overpowered the sheriff and hanged and shot Caldwell, and the coroner's jury found he died at the hands of a mob (A10, A11, A12, A5). The Register described the killing as punishment for the alleged assault and said 'an example of its swift justice was needed' (A11).

The local Iron County Register, its printing of the coroner's verdict, and several independent-seeming St. Louis wire versions agree on the jail seizure and the hanging from the railroad bridge (A4, A5, A11, A12).

accounts.label: Local paper (Iron County Register)
accounts.gist: A detailed narrative of the alleged assault, the hearing, and a sworn, disguised party of thirty or forty men who broke into the jail, hanged Caldwell from the bridge, slashed his arm and fired some thirty shots; the paper endorsed the act.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Caldwell was forcibly taken from lawful custody, hanged from the railroad bridge and shot in numerous places by a mob whose members were unknown to the jurors.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire (version 1)
accounts.gist: About a hundred men took Caldwell from the jail after his preliminary examination, hanged him to the Iron Mountain Railroad bridge and fired several shots into his body 'to make their work doubly sure.'

accounts.label: St. Louis wire (version 2)
accounts.gist: About a hundred masked men forced the jail over the jailor's refusal; Caldwell 'begged piteously for his life' and was shoved off the bridge hand rail; no shooting is mentioned.

framing.detail: The Iron County Register headed its account 'A Terrible Crime and its Reward,' called Caldwell a 'black brute,' and wrote that if any case called justly for lynch law 'this was one.'
A week later the Register's 'MOB LAW' editorial said the lynching was 'not without excuse' but warned that more mob law would not be tolerated.
Distant dailies ran the St. Louis wire under headlines such as 'A Ravisher Lynched,' 'Negro Lynched for Attempted Rape' and 'Another Negro Lynched,' presenting the accusation as fact.
Weekly news summaries reduced it to a single line naming Caldwell, Ironton and masked men.
